title: GravelLand Saga
intro: Nineteen days on gravel around southern Sweden in the summer of 2026: from Södertälje past Örebro, the Göta Canal and Lake Vänern, down the west coast to Skåne and back north along the east coast, with wild camps by the lakes.

story: The only cool moment of the day was waking up because my cat stole the blanket from my feet and a light breeze came through the open window. 😼

The adventure started with a train ride to Sodertalje and a little nervous excitement that disappeared after the first few kilometers. It turned into a beautiful mix of gravel roads and quiet pavement under a very hot summer sun. I cooled off at a fountain in a park while a curious crow tried to steal my trail snacks.
Skipped a couple of campsites until I found the perfect shelter by the lake. Evening swim, laundry, hot noodles and a fresh bun at sunset. A great first day on the road. 😊

Started early knowing storms were coming. Packed camp in 1.5 h and reached ICA just before the rain around 12. Ended up hiding in a small pizzeria for a couple of hours with a great pizza and a cold beer while the storm passed.

The afternoon was a beautiful mix of gravel roads, quiet pavement, wheat fields and wildflowers. I expected humid weather after the rain, but the ride stayed surprisingly comfortable. The pizza and beer made me sleepy for a while, but the legs came back later in the day.
Skipped five campsites before finding a peaceful lakeside spot for the night. Now it is time for dinner, a clean bike chain, a little stretching and another sunset by the water.

A warm sunrise woke me up around 6. I stayed in the tent for a while with the door open, enjoying the quiet morning before slowly packing camp. A cold swim at the lake was the perfect wake up, followed by coffee and a light breakfast in the shade beside an old abandoned boat.

The ride into Orebro was smooth with beautiful gravel paths and a peaceful waterfront where I stopped to listen to the birds. I explored the impressive castle, stocked up on zinc cream and petroleum jelly, then treated myself to a big McDonalds lunch before heading back onto the road.
From midday the headwind never really stopped. It became a day of patience more than speed, but the gravel roads, endless wheat fields and handfuls of wild strawberries made every kilometer worth it.
I reached camp early after about 74 km, found a quiet lakeside spot with a table, and now it is time to swim, wash my clothes, stretch, recover and enjoy another peaceful Swedish evening.
Another long day on the road. I woke up feeling fresh even after a midnight stomach adventure.🫠 Smecta did its job and the morning started with another beautiful sunrise.

Today had more asphalt than gravel, but Route 6 kept leading me through quiet countryside where I finally started meeting other bikepackers. It felt good knowing I was not the only one chasing long days on two wheels.🚵

A kebab stop turned into a charging session while watching cooking videos before I rolled on toward the Göta Canal. Following the canal was unforgettable. Watching boats move through the locks made me stop more than once just to enjoy the moment.🚢

One funny moment came when I had already finished half a bottle of water from a public tap before a local told me it came straight from the river. Thankfully nothing happened except a few worried thoughts.🫣

After 124 km I finally found a peaceful campsite on the shore of Lake Vänern. Waiting there was an old anchor with the inscription "Motorslupen Dux förliste här den 13 9 1938". A small memorial to a boat that sank here almost ninety years ago. Somehow it felt like the perfect ending to another day on this journey.⚓️
Another great day on the road.
I woke up beside the old Dux anchor, still amazed that yesterday's campsite had become part of the journey already.
The day started with long flat roads, open fields and plenty of sunshine. After yesterday I finally remembered to use enough sunscreen.🥵
A stop in Lidkoping meant a Burger King lunch, charging my devices and stocking up at Lidl before heading into a quieter part of Sweden.
One of today's highlights was Kinnekulle Stenbrott. What was once a limestone quarry has become a beautiful lake surrounded by walking trails. A friendly local even stopped to take a photo for me.🗿

The final climb led into the forests of Hunneberg. After another 120 km I found a cozy shelter beside the lake, surrounded by trees and silence. A perfect place to end another unforgettable day on the road.

I woke up in Hunneberg around 6.30, knowing heavy rain was forecast for the afternoon. The mosquitoes encouraged a quick pack up, and I rolled out early hoping to reach Svartedalens Nature Reserve before the worst of the weather.

Soon after leaving, my stomach started acting up again. I stopped beside the road, took some medicine and lay down for a while before continuing. The route through Vänersborg was beautiful, with peaceful waterfront paths and small rocky islands, but I was already riding with very little energy. 😮‍💨

The rolling hills never really stopped, and around noon the rain arrived. I reached the first shelter in Svartedalens, only to discover that the roof had been torn away by the wind. A temporary tarp covered the structure, but the floor was completely soaked, so I pushed on through the rain to the next shelter. 🌧

By three in the afternoon I finally arrived. I cleaned the bike with lake water after the muddy roads, serviced the drivetrain and made something simple to eat. Then I lay down, hoping to recover, but instead spent hours drifting in and out of a feverish haze without really sleeping.😵‍💫
There was almost no phone signal. I had to climb from the lakeshore up to the parking area just to send a single message home before walking back down to camp.
Later that evening I forced myself to eat a proper meal even though I had no appetite. Some days the biggest victory is simply taking care of yourself and making it to tomorrow.

I woke up beside the calm lake in Svartedalens Nature Reserve after nearly ten hours of sleep. The rain had finally stopped, but the morning began with an upset stomach. I made some tea, took Smecta and slowly packed camp, convinced that my water bottles might be causing the problem. 🤔

Leaving the forest was pure joy. My route followed a beautiful section of the European Divide Trail, where smooth gravel roads wound between quiet lakes and pine forests beneath drifting clouds. Hikers with heavy backpacks appeared here and there, making the reserve feel wonderfully alive.

I stopped at a golf club to refill my bottles with fresh drinking water, but the discomfort returned. By the time I reached Gothenburg, I decided to throw all three bottles away and replace them. Almost immediately the burping disappeared. After two frustrating days, the mystery finally seemed solved.🧐

A cheeseburger, salty fries and a cola gave me the energy I had been missing. Feeling stronger again, I left Gothenburg behind and joined Kattegattleden route, following the coast south through a small mix of gravel and quiet roads. Later I left the route and found a peaceful campsite hidden between two small lakes.
Yesterday was about survival. Today became a reminder of how quickly things can turn around when your body finally gets the chance to recover.
I woke up beside the lake before six but couldn't fall asleep again. Instead, I spent an hour listening to the quiet morning before slowly packing camp and rolling out around nine.

The first 50 km were probably the least exciting of the trip so far. Although the route follows the coast, I barely saw the sea. Instead it was mostly asphalt, traffic, railway crossings, farmland and small villages. I kept spinning easy, saving energy while meeting plenty of cyclists heading both north and south.

Closer to Varberg, the atmosphere changed completely. The waterfront was packed with people, music and what felt like a huge summer festival. I stopped for food, but my stomach had other plans and several unexpected visits to the bathroom quickly ended lunch.🫠

Beyond Varberg the coastline finally opened up. Sandy beaches, open fields and sea views made the route feel alive again. Around the 100 km mark I met two friendly bikepackers. We chatted for a while and they mentioned they were heading to a shelter with plenty of camping spots after a 15 km detour from the route. I considered joining them, but after checking where it was I decided to stay on my planned route and keep riding at my own pace.🐌

That decision turned into another 50 km before I finally reached the forests of Grimsholmen Nature Reserve and Vesslunda Nature Reserve. The first shelter was already occupied, so I climbed a little higher into the woods and found a quiet patch of soft moss for my tent, hidden from both the road and the wind.🌲
It wasn't the easiest day physically, but somehow the legs kept turning. Sometimes progress is simply trusting your own pace and letting the kilometers come one after another.🐢

After a night of heavy rain I woke up feeling surprisingly refreshed. I took my time drying the tent in the morning sun before rolling out around eleven, and for the first time in nine days the wind was finally on my side.

The French bikepacker from yesterday caught up with me again. He has been riding for four months already, and we chatted for a while before naturally drifting apart. When I asked what he remembered most from his journey, he smiled and said, "Serbia and its dogs." Apparently one day a passing car even shielded him and his girlfriend from a pack of chasing dogs. Definitely a story to remember.

Later we crossed paths once more near Tönnersa Nature Reserve, where the route finally became exactly what I had been hoping for. Sandy gravel roads, pine forests and peaceful trails made me forget the long stretches of asphalt from earlier in the trip. The coastline also became wilder. Strong waves rolled onto the shore while old windswept trees leaned toward the sea after years of battling the coastal wind.

The afternoon became a little harder as the wind shifted and the climb toward Torekov slowed me down. Every shelter I checked was already busy with other cyclists, and one even came with a warning about noisy seagulls at sunrise. Instead I trusted my luck once again, left the main route for a short detour and found a brand new shelter hidden on a quiet hillside near Förslöv. The wind now hits the outside wall while I listen to cows somewhere down in the valley.
Today felt calm. No rush, no drama, just steady progress, beautiful coastal gravel and another reminder that trusting your own rhythm is often the best route forward.
I woke up naturally at 6:30 feeling fully rested. After taking my time with breakfast and packing camp, I rolled out at 8:30 for the final ride toward Helsingborg. 🚵‍♂️

The weather was exactly what I had hoped for. Dark clouds drifted overhead, the sea was rough and alive, and after so many hot days it felt refreshing to ride under a cool grey sky. The wind couldn't decide whose side it was on, but today I honestly didn't care. The scenery was enough.😶‍🌫️
My right calf had been tight in the morning, pulling slightly on my Achilles tendon, but after giving it a proper massage the tension disappeared and the ride felt smooth again.🦵

By mid afternoon I rolled into Helsingborg, completing the second stage of this journey. The first was Södertälje to Gothenburg. The second was Gothenburg to Helsingborg. Now only the long northern return remains.

It feels like I'm roughly halfway through the adventure, still following my original plan of around 90 km per day without chasing big numbers. Tomorrow the route turns wilder again, with fewer towns, fewer shops and a little more self reliance.
Tonight is for recovery. Clean clothes, charged batteries, a comfortable bed, a pint of Guinness and a great burger to celebrate another milestone before heading back into the unknown tomorrow.🫡
Third section of the journey begins.

After a proper hotel reset yesterday, I woke up to a great breakfast, packed freshly washed gear, and rolled out without rushing. Everything had dried overnight, which already felt like a small victory.

The weather had other plans. All day long I was playing the same game: rain jacket on, rain jacket off. I probably put it on five times, and almost as often the rain stopped while I was zipping it up. Several proper showers caught me anyway, along with one burst of hail, but none of it felt miserable. The strong tailwind made riding surprisingly enjoyable despite the constantly changing weather. 🌦

The route itself has changed too. Leaving the coast behind means fewer people, fewer cyclists, less traffic, and finally the landscape I love most: rolling hills, forests and quiet country roads. It feels wilder again, more like the first section of the trip, and that's exactly what I was looking forward to. 🫶

One funny moment happened while trying to outrun a rain cloud. Another cyclist and I were pushing along with the tailwind at around 25–30 km/h, both clearly hoping to escape it. We failed. I hid beneath a huge oak tree while he stopped under the roof of a nearby school. Later, when the rain eased, I passed him again. It was actually the third time we'd crossed paths that day. He was the only touring cyclist I met all day, another reminder that this part of the route is much quieter than the coastal section.

By around 6 PM I reached today's shelter. Finally my shoes and gear had a chance to dry while another shower rolled through outside. I even had time to sketch a little, enjoy dinner, listen to the rain on the roof, and simply slow down.
Tomorrow the forecast promises sunshine and warmer weather. Hopefully I'll finish the day by a lake again, maybe even with my first swim in several days.🌊
1,000+ kilometers behind me, around 900 still to go. The adventure continues.🤠
The ride has settled into a calm rhythm, and so have I.

This third section feels very different from the coast. There may be more asphalt than gravel, but I honestly don't mind anymore. The roads are quiet, traffic is light, and they wind through endless forests and rolling hills. The weather was almost perfect today, plenty of sunshine, barely any wind, and temperatures that made riding simply enjoyable.

By around 5 PM I reached Ivö Lake. I left the main route and headed toward Kjugekull Nature Reserve before following a narrow grassy track that slowly disappeared into the forest. At the end of it I found a small sandy beach hidden behind the bushes, quiet, peaceful, and perfect for another calm night.
This evening I washed myself in the lake, did some laundry, watched everything dry in the evening sun, and simply enjoyed the silence.

I'm really happy with the pace I've found. Around 90 kilometers a day gives me enough time to ride without rushing, stop whenever something catches my eye, set up camp early, stretch, recover, and actually enjoy the places I'm passing through instead of just ticking them off on the map.

days.title: Just Ride 🌲
story: I slept early last night and woke up naturally around 7 AM, feeling completely recharged. After packing up camp, brushing a couple of ticks off the tent, and washing up, I rolled out into another beautiful day.

The first thing I noticed after leaving the shade of yesterday's forest was the heat. The sun was already strong, and by the afternoon it reached around 25–26°C. But somehow, it never felt like a battle.
Today's ride gave me plenty of time to think.
A few times I caught myself wondering whether I should take another gravel detour. But then I looked around. Quiet roads. Almost no traffic. Endless forests. Rolling hills. Beautiful scenery.
And I realized something.
If I were riding through the very same forests on gravel instead of smooth asphalt, would the experience really be any better?
Maybe not.

I still love gravel roads, but I've learned to appreciate peaceful asphalt just as much. In the end, it's not really about the surface anymore. It's about where the road takes me and how it makes me feel.

Around 88 kilometers in, I reached Lake Mien. I had marked a picnic area on the map, but it meant riding another five kilometers. Instead, I simply turned onto an unmarked forest road with no signs, no bins, no indication that anyone was there.
It turned out to be exactly what I was looking for.

A beautiful dry forest with tall trees, the lake quietly washing against the shore, and enough shade to escape the afternoon heat. I went for a long swim in the cold water, washed my clothes, serviced the bike, had dinner, and wandered along a quiet red-marked hiking trail where I met only one man walking his dog.
By five in the afternoon, camp was already set.
Right now, life feels wonderfully simple.
Sleep. Eat. Pedal. Enjoy. Repeat.
And honestly... that's all I need now.

days.title: A New Routine 🚲
story: Another morning without an alarm. I woke up around 7 AM, took my time packing camp, made breakfast, washed up, and rolled out just after 9. I've realized that this has quietly become my new daily routine.
It almost feels like a regular workday, just on a bicycle.

Wake up. Pack camp. Ride. Stop somewhere for lunch, usually a pizza or kebab place. Keep riding. Pick up groceries for dinner in the afternoon. Find a quiet place by a lake or in the forest. Set up camp. Eat. Relax. Sleep.
Then do it all again the next day.
There's something incredibly satisfying about how simple life becomes out here.

Today's ride was another peaceful one. Around 105 kilometers through quiet roads, forests and rolling countryside. I crossed paths with another fully loaded bikepacker. I'd slowly catch him on the climbs 2 times, and he'd disappear again on the flats and descents.
The biggest realization today was about the route itself.

It's called "GravelLand Saga", yet for several days now I've been riding mostly on asphalt. At first that felt a little ironic, but somewhere along the way I stopped caring about the surface beneath my tires. Gravel or asphalt.. it doesn't really matter anymore. As long as the roads are quiet, the scenery is beautiful, and I can keep moving forward, I'm exactly where I want to be. 😊

Looking at the map this evening, I realized something else. If I gently increase my daily distance over the next few days, there's a good chance I'll finish the entire journey in about 19 days. No rushing, no racing, just a steady rhythm that somehow brought me farther than I expected.
And honestly... I think I've found my pace. 🐢

days.title: Rolling Hills ☀️
story: I woke up by the lake to another beautiful morning. The tent was still damp, so I took my time drying everything before packing up and leaving camp.

As soon as I climbed away from the lake, I felt the heat. The sun was already strong, and the day quickly turned into a long sequence of rolling hills. Up, down, up again. There were finally some small gravel sections mixed into the route, which was a welcome change, but the climbing kept adding up.🌄

Finding a place to sleep turned into another small adventure. One spot was private, another was too steep and overgrown, and another turned out to be a paid parking area. At one point I even walked into the bushes, collected a few ticks on my legs, brushed them off, and decided to keep riding.

Eventually, after passing Kristdala, I simply turned off the road and found a dry spot at the edge of a forest and a field. Nothing spectacular, no lake or shelter this time, just a quiet place to sleep after a very long day.
I ate, escaped the mosquitoes into my tent, and pretty much passed out.
One interesting detail from the day: the route took me through three Swedish counties—starting in Kronoberg, briefly crossing Jönköping County, and finishing in Kalmar County.
145 km. Plenty of hills. Plenty of sun.
Sometimes the best campsite is simply the one you finally find. 🤪
After yesterday's 145 kilometers and endless rolling hills, I woke up surprisingly well rested.

The morning looked cloudy enough that I thought rain might be coming, so I packed quickly and was already riding by 8:30. The clouds didn't last long, though. The heat returned, and somewhere along the way I realized just how hungry I was.
A stop at Coop, a proper load of food, and finally a cappuccino made an immediate difference. I had probably been carrying a calorie deficit from the previous day without fully realizing it.

Today's route finally delivered plenty of gravel! Long, beautiful forest roads constantly rolling up and down, twisting left and right through the trees. After so many asphalt-heavy days, it was great to have more gravel again. But somewhere along this journey I've also stopped caring much about the surface. Asphalt or gravel, I still move at roughly the same turtle pace. 🐢
I carried a roast beef sandwich for lunch and ate it in the shade of a tree before continuing through the heat and hills.
By late afternoon I reached Västervik and stopped at MAX. A burger and cheesy fries felt like plugging myself directly into a charger. The energy came back almost immediately.🔋
There I met another bike traveler. What was supposed to be a food stop turned into a long conversation about traveling, cycling and the road ahead.😊
Eventually, I had to get moving again. I picked up a new gas canister at Jula, bought groceries, and started looking for a place to sleep.
My first planned shelter was already taken, so I continued north and reached Gränsö Nature Reserve, where I found a beautiful shelter right by the water. 🌅
Now I'm sitting here with a cup of tea, properly fed again, watching an incredible sunset over the water.
Earlier today I felt tired from the heat, the hills and probably not eating enough. Now, after good food, a good conversation and a beautiful place to end the day, I feel completely recharged.
Tomorrow begins the final stretch.
Three days to Stockholm.
Today was hot, beautiful, and full of energy.

For the first 20 km I felt incredibly fresh. I put some music on my phone and just rode, pedalling, enjoying the road, and occasionally shaking my head to the beat. After the harder days earlier in the trip, it felt great to have my nutrition properly dialled in and plenty of energy in the tank.

The route had a good mix of quiet asphalt and gravel, and somewhere around the 80–90 km mark came a very unexpected reunion. I heard someone behind me, and it was Youhe Gao , the cyclist I met yesterday. He told me he'd heard someone riding on the gravel road running parallel to the asphalt and somehow thought, “That must be him.” And it was 😄

We rode together for about an hour, talked, and even shared some gravel, despite him travelling on a road bike. Eventually I turned off toward a beautiful beach, while he continued on. We took a photo together, exchanged contacts, and wished each other a safe journey. A short encounter across two days, but definitely one of those memorable little connections that happen on a long trip.

The beach stop was exactly what I needed. I washed my clothes, cleaned myself up, swam in the lake, and even jumped from a rope swing. After days of riding in the heat, getting properly clean and cooling down felt incredible.

From there I continued toward Söderköping and finished the day at 130 km. I found a spot near the town where there are a few small shelters and pitched my tent behind one of them. Now it's coffee, dinner, bike maintenance, some stretching, and sleep.
Only two days left.

It's strange to think about how much has happened and how many kilometres have passed since Day 1. I don't even know whether I wish the trip were longer. Right now, it feels like it's lasting exactly as long as it should.
Riding 80–90 km a day would have made the final part much more relaxed, but I actually like that I added a little challenge: can I finish the whole route in 19 days?

The original plan was around 21 days, maybe more, maybe less. But somewhere along the way, 19 days became the goal. And now, with only two days left, I'm really happy that it turned out this way. It feels like exactly the right way to finish this trip.
It's hard to believe that tomorrow will be the final day of this trip.

I woke up at 7 without an alarm, as usual. Somewhere along the way, this trip gave me a pretty stable routine. Sleep around 11, wake up around 7, take my time in the morning, pack the camp, eat breakfast, have a 3-in-1 Nescafé, and ride.☕️
I felt a little beaten up when I first woke up today, but after lying in the tent for another 30 or 40 minutes, eating breakfast and slowly getting ready, I felt like myself again.

The day started with a beautiful gravel road along the canal from Söderköping. It was flat, peaceful and incredibly scenic, with boats moving along the water in both directions. The sun was already hot, but by now I think I've adapted to it. With the cool air coming from the water, it actually felt pleasant.🌬

Most of the day was surprisingly flat. Eventually I reached the ferry crossing, and the short ride across brought back memories of an old bike trip from many years ago. Back then, I finished part of the Tour Unite route in Konakovo with a ferry crossing too.

For a moment it felt like a little flashback to another life. Same bike, a different setup, and a very different version of me with much less experience. I remember being tired but happy back then. Today, I'm simply happy. Somehow, after more than 18 days on the road, I don't feel that deep accumulated exhaustion I might have expected.

After the ferry, I continued toward Nyköping. There were some asphalt sections and another excellent stretch of fast, mostly flat gravel. I also started seeing cyclists everywhere, including groups of riders with race numbers. After the quiet and isolated feeling of this third part of the trip, where I could sometimes ride all day and see only one or two other cyclists, it suddenly reminded me of the busy cycling routes along the west coast.

I reached Nyköping around 1:30 or 2 and stopped at McDonald's to refill the calorie tank and charge my phone and power banks. Then I headed back out into the heat for the final two and a half hours of the day.

Unfortunately, the road after Nyköping was probably the least enjoyable part. I somehow ended up on a busy asphalt road with constant traffic. The cars gave me space, but having them continuously rushing past still wasn't pleasant, so I just tried to get through that section as quickly as I comfortably could.🚧
And eventually I reached Lake Björken.
The shelter was already occupied by another pair of cyclists, so I walked a little farther away and found my own spot on a beautiful, relatively flat piece of ground above the shore.

And now I'm sitting here, completely clean, with freshly washed clothes, full after a good meal and a coffee. I swam in the clear lake, set up my tent, and now I'm simply enjoying the view, the nature and the last night of this trip.
I'm really happy that the journey is ending in a place like this.😍
Tomorrow, all that's left is to ride to Tumba station. From there, Stockholm is just a short train ride away.
One more day. 🤗

days.title: The Final Day
story: That's it. I made it.
I'm standing at Tumba station, waiting for the train that will take me closer to Stockholm. After that, just a short ride home.
And strangely, I don't feel anything dramatic.

There was no huge emotional finish, no overwhelming nostalgia, no big moment of realization. I simply woke up, packed my camp, got on the bike and rode. Just like I've been doing every day for the last 19 days.
Maybe it hasn't fully sunk in yet.

There was so much packed into this journey that right now it all feels mixed together. Difficult days, stomach problems, rain, headwinds, heat, endless little hills, beautiful gravel roads, quiet forests, lakes, unexpected encounters, swims, shelters, wild camps and those small moments that somehow became some of the most memorable parts of the trip.
Some days were about getting through. Some were pure enjoyment. Most were somewhere in between.
And today I simply kept pedalling until I reached Tumba.
I stopped at McDonald's on the way, had a good meal, and now I'm standing here waiting for my train. It almost feels strangely ordinary.
Maybe that's fitting.
For 19 days, this wasn't something extraordinary that I was constantly thinking about. It simply became my life. Wake up. Eat. Pack. Pedal. Explore. Find somewhere to sleep. Repeat.
And now, suddenly, it's over.
I think I'll need some time to let the whole thing settle before I understand what these 19 days really meant to me.
But for now, I know one thing.
I did it.
19 days on the road.
Home.
